query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an oxygen sublattice buffer during the bottom‐up synthesis of multi-element, near‐equiatomic HEA nanoparticles will mitigate high-temperature induced cation migration and phase segregation, thereby preserving both their structural and chemical homogeneity under service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element HEA nanoparticles synthesized by conventional bottom‐up routes without an engineered oxygen sublattice, which are prone to cation migration and phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the synthesis process by incorporating an oxygen sublattice buffer (for example, by controlled incorporation of oxide precursors that form an oxygen scaffold) during nanoparticle formation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to service regimes relevant to catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operation (473–1923 K).
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered oxygen sublattice acting as a buffer layer within the nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: The oxygen buffer is expected to stabilize the crystal lattice by reducing the mobility of cations, thereby limiting cation migration and phase segregation when subjected to high temperatures. This stabilization maintains the near-equiatomic, single-phase structure that is critical for catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to nanoparticles synthesized without the oxygen sublattice buffer, those prepared with the buffer will exhibit reduced signs of phase segregation, more uniform elemental distribution, and improved retention of catalytic or thermoelectric activity after high-temperature treatment.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles fabricated using conventional bottom-up synthesis routes in the absence of an explicit oxygen sublattice buffer.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable specifically in the context of high-temperature service regimes (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics) and may be sensitive to variations in composition or synthesis conditions beyond those controlled in the experiment.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in structural stability and the extent of performance retention are uncertain and may vary with the detailed synthesis parameters and nanoparticle composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one using the conventional bottom-up synthesis and one with the integrated oxygen sublattice buffer. Subject both sets to high-temperature aging or cycling within the specified catalytic and thermoelectric temperature ranges. Use identical metal precursor compositions and processing parameters aside from the intervention. Post-treatment, analyze the samples by structural (e.g., high-resolution TEM, XRD) and compositional (e.g., EDS mapping) methods, and assess performance metrics relevant to their catalytic and thermoelectric functions.
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to detect phase segregation.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor shifts indicative of lattice distortion or phase change.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for compositional uniformity.
Catalytic activity tests (or thermoelectric performance metrics) before and after high-temperature exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles synthesized with the oxygen sublattice buffer do not show statistically significant improvements in structural integrity (i.e., reduced phase segregation and cation migration) or in retention of catalytic/thermoelectric performance compared to the control samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Inspired by rocksalt HEOs, researchers have undertaken extensive work to develop diverse types of HEOs. HEOs in different crystal structures have been synthesized accordingly in the past decade, such as fluorite (, ), perovskite (), spinel (), bixbyite (), and pyrochlore (, ). reading.lever: Integrate an oxygen sublattice buffer during nanoparticle synthesis to mitigate cation migration and phase segregation at high temperatures.
reading.why: Because the bottom-up synthesis of HEOs with an oxygen sublattice has shown improved structural robustness, suggesting a promising adaptation for stabilizing HEA nanoparticles under service temperatures.
